newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish prime minister reproaches EU over trade.
newsitem.headline: Polish prime minister reproaches EU over trade.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz criticised the European Union (EU) on Thursday for its alleged protectionism following a row between Poland and Spain over citrus fruit.

Cimoszewicz said Poland, hoping the join the union soon after 2000, had opened up many areas to competition from EU countries, even though its economy was much weaker, and some of these moves had remained unreciprocated.

"In my opinion Poland has made many steps..., gestures towards the EU in various difficult, controversial areas and not in all cases did we experience the same attitude from the other side," he told Reuters in an interview.

Cimoszewicz said he was disappointed with EU's failure to deliver financial help for Poland's steel industry, which it had offered in exchange for Warsaw dropping plans to protect the industry with high duties for a longer period.
The deal was agreed last year during a visit to Warsaw of European Commissioner Hans van den Broek, he said.

"Poland decided not to implement its earlier plan to apply stronger customs protection to the steel sector in connection with van den Broek's promise that the EU would present a plan of financial assistance for modernisation of the industry within six months," Cimoszewicz said.
"It now seems the EU is not eager to meet this promise, various agruments appear, new standpoints. This is a disappointing attitude," he said.
He said EU's advantage in trade relations was highlighted by Warsaw's large trade deficit with EU countries, amounting to 60 percent of its total trade gap of $8.2 billion last year.

Cimoszewicz said Poland was vulnerable to unfair demands of privileges in trade by some EU countries during the current sensitive period as it awaits the European Commission's opinion on how well it is prepared for EU membership, a so-called avis.

He said one such demand was Spain's insistence that Poland scrap its 22-percent value-added tax on imported citrus fruits, which would cost the budget some 200 million zlotys ($65 million) in lost revenues.

He said some Spanish members of the European Commission, the EU's executive body, had threatened to block the work of next week's Association Council, during which Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati will meet his EU counterparts.

"I believe this will not happen...If Spain wanted to bloc the efficiency of the Association Council, this would be most disappointing because it would raise a question about Spain's attitude to EU's expansion," he said.
"So far all Spanish politicians I met declared such support," he said.

At the Council's meeting, Warsaw and Brussels are widely expected to end disputes over car assembly regulations in Poland, Polish recognition of European Union product certificates and an understanding on Poland's fuels sector.
